## The case

You are the data analyst on a small study. Your client is the channel manager at a small creator
agency that represents about a dozen Twitch streamers. The agency is about to pitch a sponsor on
how engaged its streamers' chats are. Before the pitch, the manager wants three questions
answered with data:

1. Does chat in gaming channels look different from chat in non-gaming channels?
2. Does a bigger audience change how people write?
3. How much of chat is reaction (an emote, a cheer, a single word) and how much is commentary?

**Where the job stands.** In Data Wrangling you built the table, `data/twitch_analysis.RDS`,
with your thirty hand-coded messages inside it. The manager has not seen a number from it yet.

**Your job.** Show the manager what is in the table before anything is tested: how often each
category occurs, how long messages run, how two categories line up, and what the patterns look
like in a chart. The manager does not read R, so every **Write:** prompt is a note to them.

## Your assignment

| Part | What you do | Why the client needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Frequency tables: count how often each category occurs | The manager sees how much of chat is gaming, large-audience, and reaction |
| 2 | The three numbers: the mean, median, and standard deviation of message length | "How people write" becomes numbers the manager can compare |
| 3 | The cross-tabulation: count viewer band against channel type | The manager sees whether audience size and channel type go together |
| 4 | Three figures, each with alt text, a disclosure sentence, and an interpretation | A chart is what the manager can put in front of a sponsor |
| Last | Explain this stage to the client, in one short paragraph | The manager gets what you found in plain language |

The code sits in gray boxes called chunks, as in Data Wrangling. Work through them in order:

1. Replace each blank, shown as `___`, with the code it needs.
2. Click **Run Cell** at the top left of the gray box.
3. Compare what R prints with **What you should see**.

Where the worksheet says **Write:**, type your answer in your own words. Every task has a
**Help** link. It opens the page that explains that task: what the blank needs, where to click,
and what to do when R prints an error.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)     # tables and charts
library(v2v)           # theme_v2v() and the course palette
options(scipen = 10)  # long numbers such as timestamps print in full; p-values keep the usual form
analysis <- read_rds("data/twitch_analysis.RDS")  # the table worksheet 1 saved
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)        # where every chart is saved
analysis %>% count(reaction_only)  # your hand-coded variable made it through
```

**What you should see:** your two coded groups adding to `30`, and `NA` with `35237`.
[Help with Setup](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#setup)

## Part 1: Frequency tables

### Task 1.1: Channel type

A frequency table says how often each category occurs. This one is done for you as the model.

```{r}
#| label: freq-channel-type
analysis %>%
  count(channel_type) %>%                  # messages per category
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))  # and as a share of all messages
```

**What you should see:** `gaming` `31309` (88.8%), `non-gaming` `3457` (9.8%), and `NA` `501`
(1.4%).
[Help with Task 1.1](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-1-1)

### Task 1.2: Viewer band

Build the same table for `viewer_band`.

```{r}
#| label: freq-viewer-band
analysis %>%
  count(viewer_band) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

**What you should see:** `small` `27766` (78.7%), `medium` `5501` (15.6%), `large` `2000` (5.7%).
[Help with Task 1.2](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-1-2)

### Task 1.3: Your hand-coded variable

Only thirty messages carry a code. Keep those rows first, or the table is mostly `NA`.

```{r}
#| label: freq-reaction
analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(reaction_only)) %>%  # only the thirty coded messages
  count(reaction_only) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

**What you should see:** two rows adding to `30`.
[Help with Task 1.3](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-1-3)

**Write:** two to three sentences for the client on the three tables: what they show, and what
they do not. Name the numbers.

These tables show that of the messages, 88.8% are from gaming channels while 9.8% are from non-gaming channels. Around half of the dataset are coded as commentary, at 16 (53.3%), while 14 of the 30 are coded as reaction (46.7%). The viewer band table shows that most of the messages are from small channels, 78.7%. Then 15.6% are from medium channels, and 5.7% from large channels. Though, these tables do not make any inferences about the data and the way they are related.

## Part 2: The three numbers

### Task 2.1: Message length, all messages

```{r}
#| label: length-all
analysis %>%
  summarize(
    n      = sum(!is.na(message_length)),
    mean   = mean(message_length, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(message_length, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = sd(message_length, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

**What you should see:** `n` `35263`, `mean` `29.0`, `median` `17`, `sd` `41.2`.
[Help with Task 2.1](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-2-1)

### Task 2.2: By channel type, and by your code

Fill the grouping variable, then the filter that keeps only your coded messages.

```{r}
#| label: length-by-group
analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(channel_type)) %>%
  group_by(channel_type) %>%
  summarize(
    n      = n(),
    mean   = mean(message_length, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(message_length, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = sd(message_length, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(reaction_only)) %>%
  group_by(reaction_only) %>%

  summarize(
    n      = n(),
    mean   = mean(message_length),
    median = median(message_length),
    sd     = sd(message_length),
    max    = max(message_length)
  )
```

**What you should see:** `gaming` n `31309`, mean `28.5`, median `17`, sd `38.5`; `non-gaming`
n `3457`, mean `33.7`, median `16`, sd `60.7`. Then one row for each of your two coded groups.
[Help with Task 2.2](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-2-2)

**Write:** two to three sentences for the client. Where do the mean and the median disagree, and
what does the gap tell you about the shape of message length?

*Your answer:*
For the commentary messages, the mean is 30.1 whole the median is 21, which are fairly close to each other. This shows that there aren't many outliers in the commentary messages, and both give a good representation of the data. The reaction messages have a mean of 15.6 and a median of 9, which is a larger gap. This shows that there are some outliers in the reaction messages, so the median is a better representation of the data. Both message types have a right-skewed distribution, but the reaction messages moreso than the commentary messages.

## Part 3: The cross-tabulation

### Task 3.1: Viewer band by channel type

```{r}
#| label: crosstab
analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(channel_type)) %>%
  count(viewer_band, channel_type) %>%                   # viewer band as the rows, channel type as the columns
  pivot_wider(names_from = channel_type, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)   # one column per channel type
```

**What you should see:** three rows of counts. `small`: `25309` gaming, `2457` non-gaming.
`medium`: `4000` and `1000`. `large`: `2000` and `0`.
[Help with Task 3.1](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-3-1)

### Task 3.2: As proportions of each band

The same counts as shares of each band.

```{r}
#| label: crosstab-shares
analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(channel_type)) %>%
  count(viewer_band, channel_type) %>%
  group_by(viewer_band) %>%                           # shares within each band, not across the table
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3))
```

**What you should see:** non-gaming is `0.088` of the small band and `0.2` of the medium band.
The large band has no non-gaming row.
[Help with Task 3.2](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-3-2)

**Write:** two to three sentences for the client on the cross-tabulation. What does it show, and
what can it not show yet?

*Your answer:*
The cross-tabulation shows the highest amount of messages are from small gaming channels, with 25,309 messages (0.912 share). The medium band has 4,000 messages from gaming channels (0.08 share) versus the non-gaming channels with 1,000 messages (0.2 share). And there are only gaming channels in the large band, with 2,000 messages. This tells us that gaming channels of all sizes are more common versus non-gaming channels, but it does not yet explain why this difference exists or if it is important enough to be considered.

## Part 4: Figures

Each figure is built, saved to `figures/` by the code that makes it, and carries alt text you
write on its `#| fig-alt:` line. After each one, **Write:** one sentence disclosing a choice you
made in it (a cap on an axis, which categories you kept, a bin width), and two to three
sentences of interpretation for the client.

### Task 4.1: Channel type within each viewer band

A proportion bar chart of the cross-tabulation. Fill the fill aesthetic and the position that
makes every bar the same height.

```{r}
#| label: fig-band-type
#| fig-alt: "YOUR TURN: one sentence saying what this chart shows."
fig_band_type <- analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(channel_type)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = viewer_band, fill = channel_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +                        # every bar scaled to 100%
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_v2v() +
  labs(title   = "Channel type within each viewer band",
       x       = "Viewer band (channel's median viewers)",
       y       = "Share of messages",
       fill    = "Channel type",
       caption = "Source: v2v Twitch corpus, November 18 to 24, 2018. 501 messages with no channel type left out.") +
  theme_v2v()

fig_band_type
ggsave("figures/band-by-type.png", fig_band_type, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

**What you should see:** three bars of equal height, and `band-by-type.png` in `figures/`.
[Help with Task 4.1](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-4-1)

**Write:** the disclosure sentence, then two to three sentences of interpretation.

*Your answer:*
This chart shows the percentage shares of messages depending on channel type and sorted by viewer band. Since no large non-gaming channels are in the dataset, the Large band is 100% gaming. The medium band has the highest percentage of non-gaming channels at 20% while the small band has only 8.8%. Still, the gaming channels dominate every band.

### Task 4.2: Message length by your code

The thirty coded messages, as a boxplot. Fill the variable on the x axis and the geom.

```{r}
#| label: fig-length-reaction
#| fig-alt: "YOUR TURN: one sentence saying what this chart shows."
fig_length_reaction <- analysis %>%
  filter(!is.na(reaction_only)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reaction_only, y = message_length)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +   # no outlier dots here; the points below show every message
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +   # every one of the thirty, shown as a point
  labs(title   = "Message length by message type",
       x       = "Hand-coded message type",
       y       = "Characters",
       caption = "Source: 30 hand-coded messages, 15 each from bobross and giantwaffle.") +
  theme_v2v()

fig_length_reaction
ggsave("figures/length-by-reaction.png", fig_length_reaction, width = 6, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

**What you should see:** two boxes, and `length-by-reaction.png` in `figures/`.
[Help with Task 4.2](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-4-2)

**Write:** the disclosure sentence, then two to three sentences of interpretation.

*Your answer:*
This chart shows how message type, wether commentary or reaction, connect to the length of the message. The commentary messages tend to have a higher message length than the reaction messages do, and more extreme outliers. The reaction messages have fevwer extreme outliers, and the median is lower than that of the commentary messages. This makes sense because reaction messages are coded as such when they are a single word or cheer, while commentary messages are coded as such if there are more than two words.

### Task 4.3: A figure of your own choice

Choose the variable and the chart, and let the R Companion write it. Then fill in its title, axis
labels, and caption, and keep the `fig_own <-` and `ggsave()` lines so the figure is saved.
[Help with Task 4.3](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/resources/help/describing-data.html#task-4-3)

```{r}
#| label: fig-own
#| fig-alt: "YOUR TURN: one sentence saying what this chart shows."
fig_own <- analysis %>%
filter(message_length <= 200) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = message_length)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  # Write the counts with commas (12,000), not 12000.
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Message length",
    subtitle = "Messages up to 200 characters",
    x = "Characters per message",
    y = "Messages",
    caption = "Source: v2v package, November 2018 Twitch collection",
    alt = "YOUR TURN: one sentence saying what the chart shows, for a reader who cannot see it."
  ) +
  v2v::theme_v2v()

# Save the chart to a picture file in your figures folder.
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave("figures/message-length-histogram.png", width = 7, height = 5)

fig_own
ggsave("figures/own-choice.png", fig_own, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

**Write:** one sentence on why you chose this chart for this variable, the disclosure sentence,
and two to three sentences of interpretation.


```{r}
#| fig-alt: "YOUR TURN: the same one sentence as alt in labs() below."
# ---- Histogram: how one number is spread out ----
# Each bar counts the messages whose length falls in a 5-character band. Lengths over 200
# are dropped from the picture only, so the long tail does not squash the bars.
analysis %>%
  filter(message_length <= 200) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = message_length)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  # Write the counts with commas (12,000), not 12000.
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Message length",
    subtitle = "Messages up to 200 characters",
    x = "Characters per message",
    y = "Messages",
    caption = "Source: v2v package, November 2018 Twitch collection",
    alt = "YOUR TURN: one sentence saying what the chart shows, for a reader who cannot see it."
  ) +
  v2v::theme_v2v()

# Save the chart to a picture file in your figures folder.
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave("figures/message-length-histogram.png", width = 7, height = 5)
```


*Your answer:*

*Your answer:*

I noticed some big outliers in message length, so I wanted a different visual for how they are distributed, which has given a very interesting result. The majority of the messages are under 50 characters, and there is a big spike at around 10 characters, with 8,000 messages falling into that range. Though many are not under that range either. I think this makes sense because many messages are just a few words, so they would fall into a shorter amount of characters without being only one or two. Longer messages are also likely not as common because twitch chats move so quickly and are live, so it is harder for a longer message to stay relevant by the time it is sent, and it is harder for others to read and reply to it.


## Explain this stage to the client

**Write:** one short paragraph, in plain language, that you would send to the channel manager.
Say what you did at this stage (what you counted, measured, and charted), what it shows about
the three questions they asked, and what it does not show yet: a description says how the
numbers sit, not whether a difference is bigger than chance, and that is worksheet 3. No R, no
column names, no jargon the manager would have to look up. Name the numbers that matter to
them.

*Your paragraph:*
At this stage I counted and compared the number of messages between gaming and non-gaming channels, the number of messages between small, medium, and large channels, and the number of messages coded as commentary versus reaction. I also measured message length compared to these factors. I found that gaming channels are both more common and have more messages in the dataset. The amount if commentary versus reaction messages is about even, with a larger variety of message lengths in the commentary messages. The highest messages are from small gaming channels with 25,309 messages. This does not yet show if these differences are big enough to matter, though I can infer that some differences, while not all, will probably tell us something significant.
